newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss pension fund assets continue growth.
newsitem.headline: Swiss pension fund assets continue growth.

text.p: Swiss private pension fund assets are forecast to grow by more than 15 percent in 1997 thanks to net inflows and booming markets, a leading banking analyst said.

Hans Kaufmann of Julius Baer Bank, in an industry study published this week, also predicted higher demand for Swiss equities by both foreign and Swiss pension funds hunting for high returns to provide pensioners with secure living standards.
Kaufmann said Swiss private pension funds had 360 billion Swiss francs ($249.8 billion) under management, up from 315 billion at end-1995.

This makes them a bigger investor than Swiss mutual funds, which had 251 billion Swiss francs under management at end-May according to fund statistician Bopp ISB in Switzerland's estimated $1.8 trillion asset management industry.
"The Swiss private pension fund industry is growing and growing," Kaufmann told Reuters.
Pension fund managers say assets grew by around 10 percent in 1996 and report continuing net inflows to the industry despite Switzerland's weak economy and ageing population.
Kaufmann said the capital stock of Swiss private pension funds built over the years, including from foreign investors, had soared to 225 percent of the Swiss Gross Domestic Product.
Swiss private pension fund investments in domestic stocks are expected to rise from their current level of an estimated 16 percent of the Swiss stock market capitalisation, he predicted.
He said future growth would also be fuelled by state pension funds of big public-owned sectors such as the Swiss telecoms firm, Telecom PTT, and railways, yet to tap the markets fully.

"Swiss pension funds, life insurance companies and investment funds have a large need for investment paper each year...because each year there are considerable earnings which have to be reinvested," Kaufmann's study said.
Coupled with foreign pension funds hunting for profitable Swiss shares, this will send prices even higher, Kaufmann said.
"The problems of social security are increasing not only on the financial side but also on the investment side," he said.
"If interest rates in Switzerland and the rest of Europe stay low, pressure to undertake more profitable investment will increase massively although this would involve greater risks."
Swiss private pension funds are increasing stock holdings, more than 80 percent Swiss and the remainder foreign shares.

Kaufmaann said the share of equities in portfolios had doubled in the past 10 years to 16 percent, but lagged behind life assurance and pension providers elsewhere which invest mainly in shares to build up wealth to provide for retirement.
Swiss private pension fund portfolios are invested in bonds by some 28 percent, followed by real estate by 24 percent, he said. The share of loans to employees was around 15 percent.
Among the market giants are the pharmaceuticals group Novartis and electrical engineering firm ABB Asia Brown Boveri.
The state system including the government retirement scheme (AHV), which has invested assets of nearly 30 billion Swiss francs, has missed recent market booms, Kaufmann said.
An ageing population, longer life expectancy and only modest pay rises will bring more trouble as the government tries to review the heavy burden on employees and taxpayers, he said.
Kaufmann's study showed that the share of indirect and direct taxes in Swiss household revenues had jumped to 36 percent of income from wages alone in 1996 from 25 percent in 1980.

The state cannot sustain unfunded pensions when early retirement is spreading faster than expected and the ratio of workers to those in retirement is forecast to slump to two in 2040 from three now and compared to 4.4 in 1960, Kaufmann added.
--- Elif Kaban, Reuters Geneva Newsroom 41-22-733 38 31 ($ = 1.441 Swiss Francs)
